facts: A rural road built by a municipality, running across the slope above a national highway, has failed. Debris has come down onto the national highway and blocked it.
why: the FAILING asset is the municipal rural road; asset-anchored routing must name its owner, not the highway's

facts: The national highway itself is blocked by debris from a slope failure above it. Traffic is stopped and vehicles are queued.
why: an event has occurred on a national highway; emergency duty sits with the district committee

facts: A tension crack has opened in the slope beside a rural road inside a rural municipality. The road is still passable.
why: no event yet; the ward's maintenance duty for landslides in local roads applies

facts: A landslide has covered a village road inside a municipality. No vehicles can pass.
why: clearance is an emergency duty of the local disaster committee

facts: Debris and flood water are blocking a local road within a ward of a rural municipality after heavy rain.
why: floods and landslides in roads are expressly the ward's and the local committee's duty

facts: A cutting on a national highway shows a new tension crack and a small slump. The carriageway is open.
why: national highways are federal; the road division office owns maintenance

facts: Falling debris from a slope on a national highway is landing on the shoulder. The road remains open but is narrowing.
why: no blockage yet; this is a maintenance duty of the road division office

facts: A state highway maintained by the provincial government has a slope failure on one side.
why: state highways are a provincial competence

facts: A state highway under the province is blocked by a landslide.
why: emergency duty is the district chain whatever tier owns the road; only permanent repair differs

facts: A river is eroding its bank and threatening a settlement. Earlier check dams and gabions have failed.
why: river training and bank protection sit with the water-induced disaster department

facts: A debris flow has come down a torrent beside a settlement and the bank is cutting away.
why: landslide and torrent control on watercourses is the water-induced disaster department's programme

facts: A steep privately owned hillside above a house has developed cracks. The landowner has refused to take any action.
why: the municipality can act on structures and land use; the power to compel stabilisation of a bare slope is a documented legal gap

facts: A building on private land is at risk because the ground behind it is moving. The owner will not act.
why: demolition and cost recovery powers reach buildings and structures

facts: The slope immediately behind a community basic-level school is unstable and cracks are appearing in the playground.
why: basic education is a local competence, so the local level owns the asset

facts: Ground movement is threatening a local health post building.
why: basic health is a local competence

facts: The district authorities need to issue a public warning that landslides are likely across the district in the coming days.
why: issuing public warnings is the hydrology and meteorology department's function with national dissemination

facts: A municipality wants an independent geological opinion on whether a slope is stable enough to build on.
why: engineering-geology opinion is the mines and geology department's role, as an opinion source only

facts: Several agencies must coordinate a district-wide landslide response across multiple municipalities.
why: the district disaster committee coordinates across local levels

facts: A slope somewhere in the hills may or may not be unstable. Nothing specific is known.
why: no asset, no event and no jurisdiction: routing must abstain rather than guess

facts: A road is affected by something.
why: no ownership clue and no event type; guessing would risk misrouting a national highway to a ward

facts: There is a problem near a river.
why: insufficient to distinguish bank erosion from a local drainage complaint
